title: The Kings
subtitle: Nine crowns and the manners of Hell
blurb: A royal procession: the king on the camel whose roar cannot be understood, the monster you must take your hat off to, and the beautiful one who lies.

segments.t: Listen. Before anything comes into view, there is a sound. Trumpets, a long way off. Then cymbals, bright and badly behaved. Then, underneath both, something that might be a voice, if a voice could be the size of a hillside. That is how you know a king of Hell is coming. You hear him long before you see him.

Last night we walked the courts. Ranks, metals, legions. Tonight we stand still and let the top of it come to us. Nine spirits in this book carry the title of king. Their seals are meant to be made in gold, the metal of the sun. So think of tonight as a procession. You are at the edge of the circle. Stay behind the line, and watch them pass.

Two of the nine you know already. Bael came through on the first night, hoarse, wearing a cat and a toad and a man all at once. Beleth rode past on the third, on a pale horse, in a fury, with his own band playing. Nod to them. They will not nod back. Now look west. The noise is getting louder, and the one making it is the most famous king in the book.
The Ninth Spirit in this Order is Paimon, a Great King, and very obedient unto Lucifer. He appeareth in the form of a Man sitting upon a Dromedary with a Crown most glorious upon his head.

Paimon. A king, and a great one. Two hundred legions follow him, the largest army in the whole book. He comes as a man on a dromedary, which is a camel with one hump, the fast kind. And ahead of him walks a host of spirits shaped like men, with trumpets, cymbals and every sort of instrument. A king who travels with his own orchestra. His seal is in your grimoire now.
He hath a great Voice, and roareth at his first coming, and his speech is such that the Magician cannot well understand unless he can compel him.

I think that is the best stage direction in the book. He arrives roaring, in a voice so large that the words will not come apart into sense. The magician has to compel him to speak plainly. Until then it is only weather. All that music, that crown, that patient camel, and a king shouting something enormous at you that you cannot follow.

And once he is made plain, what does he give? He teaches all arts and sciences, and secret things. He gives dignity, meaning rank, and confirms it. He can bind any man to the magician's will. And he gives good familiars, which are lesser spirits lent out as servants or tutors. He is to be looked for toward the west. Then the book makes a promise.
He can discover unto thee what the Earth is, and what holdeth it up in the Waters; and what Mind is, and where it is; or any other thing thou mayest desire to know.

What the earth is, and what holds it up. What mind is, and where it is. I find it touching that a book of demons saves its grandest king for the questions a curious child would ask first. Paimon is the best known of the nine today, well beyond readers of old books. Why that happened is a story for the eleventh night.

threshold.q: While he passes, let me ask you something. Paimon will tell you one thing, plainly, with the roar turned off. What do you ask him?

opts.label: What holds the earth up
opts.reply: The practical one. In the sixteen hundreds that was a live question, and the honest answer was that nobody in the room knew. We would tell you now that nothing holds it up. It falls forever around the sun. I suspect Paimon would enjoy saying that to a man standing in a chalk circle.

opts.label: Where the mind is
opts.reply: Ah. You want the hard one. Four centuries on, with machines that can watch a brain at work, people still argue about what a mind even is. If the king on the camel knows, he has kept it to himself. I would ask the same, and I would not expect a comfortable answer.

opts.label: Why all the trumpets
opts.reply: A fair question, and a sharp one. The trumpets are there because a king without a noise is only a man on a camel. Every court on earth has known that. The people who imagined Hell could not imagine power arriving quietly. That tells you a good deal about power, and nothing whatever about Hell.

segments.t: Keep your question. The music is fading west, and the next king is already at the line. Fewer trumpets, more teeth. He also comes with the strangest rule of manners in the whole book, so stand up straight.

Asmoday. A king, with seventy-two legions. He has three heads. One of a bull, one of a man, one of a ram. He has a serpent's tail, and feet webbed like a goose, and flames come out of his mouth. He sits on an infernal dragon, and in his hand he carries a lance with a banner on it, like a knight at a tournament. The book calls him first and choicest under Amaymon, one of the great kings of the quarters from last night.

Now the rule. The book says that whoever calls him must stand on his feet the whole time, with his cap or headdress off. Bareheaded. If the cap stays on, Amaymon will deceive him and all his work will be betrayed. The book's word for the magician is exorcist, which in these pages means the one who commands a spirit. So. Three heads and goose feet are riding a dragon toward you. And the instruction is, take off your hat.
But as soon as the Exorcist seeth Asmoday in the shape aforesaid, he shall call him by his Name, saying: Art thou Asmoday? and he will not deny it, and by-and-by he will bow down unto the ground.

That is an introduction at court. You uncover your head, you ask his name, he owns it, he bows. Then come the gifts. He gives something called the Ring of Virtues. He teaches arithmetic, astronomy, geometry and every handicraft. He answers truly and fully. He makes a person invincible, and he shows where treasure lies, and guards it. His name is far older than this book. That story is waiting on the ninth night.

Now the procession quickens. Four kings, close together, and you will notice they share a wardrobe. First, Purson. A king, with twenty-two legions. A comely man with the face of a lion, riding a bear, holding a cruel viper in his hand, and many trumpets sounding before him. He knows all hidden things. He finds treasure. He tells past, present and future. He answers truly about earthly things, secret and divine, and about the creation of the world, and he brings good familiars. A lion's face on a bear's back, and what he sells is an honest answer.

Behind him, Vine. A king and also an earl, with thirty-six legions. He comes as a lion riding a black horse, with a viper in his hand. Two lions and two vipers in a row. Vine discovers hidden things, and witches and wizards, and things present, past and to come. He is also the engineer of the nine.
He, at the command of the Exorcist will build Towers, overthrow Great Stone Walls, and make the Waters rough with Storms.

Towers up, walls down, storms on the water. Then Balam, a king with forty legions. Three heads again, a bull, a man and a ram, the same three as Asmoday. A serpent's tail. Flaming eyes. He rides a furious bear, carries a goshawk on his fist like a gentleman out hunting, and speaks with a hoarse voice. He gives true answers about things past, present and to come, and he makes men invisible, and witty.

And last of the four, Zagan. A king and a president, with thirty-three legions. He comes first as a bull with the wings of a griffin, and after a while he puts on a human shape. He makes men witty. Then he does a trick that would have made a reader in the sixteen hundreds sit very still, because they knew exactly whose miracle it was.
He can turn Wine into Water, and Blood into Wine, also Water into Wine. He can turn all Metals into Coin of the Dominion that Metal is of. He can even make Fools wise.

Water into wine, and wine back into water, which seems unkind. Metal into the coin of the realm, which is thoughtful. And then the quiet one at the end. He can even make fools wise. Of everything on offer tonight, that may be the one miracle nobody has ever managed to buy.

Step back from the line a moment and count the gifts. Knowledge. Hidden things found. True answers. Wit. Dignities, which are ranks and offices. Almost nobody tonight has offered to hurt anyone. This is my reading, not the manuscripts. I think the list is a mirror. It shows what a clever, obscure person in the sixteen hundreds wanted and could not get. An education. A patron. A place at court.

threshold.q: So let me hold that mirror up to you. One royal gift, tonight only, no questions asked. Which do you take?

opts.label: A place at court
opts.reply: Rank, then. A seat at the table and a door that opens when you knock. Most of the people who copied this book would have chosen the same, and they would have been ashamed to say so. You are not. Good. Wait for the last king before you sign anything.

opts.label: The coin, thank you
opts.reply: Sensible. Money is the one gift on the list you could check with your teeth. I notice Zagan pays in local currency, which suggests whoever wrote his entry had been cheated by a moneychanger at least once. Take the coin. Count it twice.

opts.label: Make the fools wise
opts.reply: The generous answer. I note you did not say which fools. That is the charm of it. Everyone who asks Zagan for this gift has somebody else in mind, and the book, very tactfully, does not say where he begins. I hope it works. I hope it is painless.

segments.t: Hold on to it. There is one king left, and you may want to count your change after him. The trumpets have stopped. He rides no animal. He comes in fire, and he is the most beautiful thing in the procession.

He appeareth in the Form of Two Beautiful Angels sitting in a Chariot of Fire. He speaketh with a Comely Voice, and declareth that he fell first from among the worthier sort, that were before Michael, and other Heavenly Angels.

Belial. A mighty king, created, the book says, next after Lucifer. He appears as two beautiful angels sitting in a chariot of fire, and he speaks with a comely voice. He commands eighty legions in the text I am following. The printings disagree, and some say fifty. Even his soldiers will not hold still.

You have met him before. On the first night, when the brass vessel was broken open and the spirits flew home, one did not go. Belial slipped into a statue and answered the people who sacrificed to it. Now look at what he gives. Presentations and senatorships. A presentation was the right to name a priest to a paid post in a church. A senatorship is a seat in government. He hands out jobs. He wins you the favour of friends and of foes, and he gives excellent familiars.

Here is the catch, and it is a courtier's catch. Belial must be given offerings, sacrifices and gifts, or he will not answer truly at all. And even paid, the book warns, he does not stay one hour in the truth unless divine power holds him to it. So the most beautiful king, the one with the best jobs to give, has to be bribed, and lies anyway. Whoever wrote that had been to court.

That is the procession. Nine crowns, and you have seen them all. Notice how courtly it was. Hats off. Names asked and given. Bows, banners, bands, presents for the great man. The people who copied this book could picture Hell quite easily. It looked like the palace they were never invited into.

Tomorrow we leave the throne room for somewhere quieter. A surprising number of the spirits in this book are teachers. They offer philosophy, logic, medicine, the languages of birds. We will call the night The Faculty, and I will show you a Hell that looks very like a university.
Until then. The kings have gone by, and seven new seals are in your grimoire. And if you find yourself in grand company this week, remember the rule. Stand up. Cap off. Ask the name.

glossary.def: A one-humped camel, the swift riding kind. Paimon's mount in the Goetia, and the reason he is so easy to recognise in old illustrations.
An attendant spirit said to serve a magician. Several spirits of the Goetia are described as giving good familiars.
In the Goetia, simply the magician: the person who calls and commands a spirit. The modern meaning, someone who drives a spirit out, came to dominate later.
Ranks, titles and offices. When the book says a spirit gives dignities, it means worldly promotion: a post, a title, a place at court.
Belial's gifts. A presentation was the right to appoint a clergyman to a paid church living; a senatorship is a seat in government. In plain terms, good jobs.
